highlights.text: the rising or curving upward of something
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core idea for the root

highlights.text: Al-ḥadab means high ground — a hillock or elevation.
two roots: first, prevention (al-manʿ); second, the edge of a thing.
The ḥadd is the barrier between two things.
Iron (ḥadīd) is named for its resistance, hardness and toughness.
Muḥādda means opposing someone, as if it were mutual withholding.
Al-Nābigha has the King (al-malīk) tell Sulaymān to "restrain (uḥdud) creation from folly".
Al-Aʿshā speaks of a dark wine-jar "kept by its ḥaddād".
The ḥadd for a disobedient person is called ḥadd because it prevents him from repeating the act.
one core sense: something encircling or surrounding something else.
Land covered with trees.
Illustrated with a line of verse: death "encircled" the poet while his supporters were slow to arrive.
a thing's coming into being after it was not — newness, coming-to-pass.
"speech / report": tied to the same root
tending to or watching over something.
guarding, keeping, preserving. حَفِظَ الشَّيْءَ = to guard or keep a thing (verbal noun ḥifẓ).
lightness/swiftness in work, and gathering/coming-together.
Ibn Fāris surveys three readings of ḥafadah: helpers/attendants
the qunūt supplication phrase "ilayka nasʿā wa naḥfidu"
a kind of sound, one thing going round another, and hardship in living.
Ibn Fāris cites Q 39:75, "and you will see the angels surrounding (ḥāffīn)
with a line of Ṭarafa: "As though the two wings of a maḍraḥī (a large bird of prey) flanked its two sides
ḥafr — digging something, i.e. removing or pulling it out from underneath.
"the beginning of a matter."
Al-ḥafar is the earth dug out of a pit
used in Qur'an 79:10 — "Are we indeed to be returned to al-ḥāfira?" Ibn Fāris reports this is explained as "the first/original state,"
"Payment at the hoof" (al-naqdu ʿinda al-ḥāfir): the horse doesn't leave until you've paid its price.
"Aḥfānī" = he wore me down by relentless pressing or repeated asking.
describes someone gentle and solicitous toward you, who treats you kindly and takes warm interest in you (yaḥtafī bika).
Q19:47, "innahu kāna bī ḥafiyyan" — glossed there as "dutiful, gentle."
al-Aʿshā (swearing not to pity a mount's "footsoreness")
a single primitive meaning (barring) generates the anatomical and celestial vocabulary through visual resemblance
"I barred him from such-and-such," which he glosses simply as "I prevented him."
the internal partition that screens off the heart from the rest of the body cavity
ḥ-j-j has four distinct root meanings
In his words, "every qaṣd is ḥajj".
Ḥājajtuhu fa-ḥajajtuhu means "I argued with him and beat him with proof"; this is winning in a dispute.
Abū Dhuʾayb uses ḥajīj for a wound so treated.
prevention/withholding (manʿ) together with encompassing or surrounding a thing (iḥāṭa).
al-ḥajar — "stone"; smaller-number plural aḥjār, also the rare pattern ḥijāra
ḥijr = the intellect/reason, so called because it holds one back from improper action
Ibn Fāris connects this to the Qur'anic ḥijran maḥjūran (al-Furqān 25:22)
Shāhid: Labīd, "a huge, powerful she-camel waters the gardens."
ḥajara l-ḥākimu ʿalā s-safīh — "the judge placed a ban on the incompetent man," i.e. barred him from disposing of his own property.
al-ḥajz: to prevent or separate two things by placing a barrier between them.
Cited: Qur'an 27:61, "And He placed between the two seas a barrier (ḥājizan)."
69:47: "there is not one among you who could hold it back (ḥājizīn)."
Proverb: "If you want mutual restraint (al-muḥājaza)
prevention or restraint (al-manʿ).
Judgement/authority (al-ḥukm) is the primary derivative
Wisdom (al-ḥikma) belongs to the same pattern, because it restrains a person from ignorance (jahl).
a line of Ṭarafa, where muḥakkam denotes the wise elder.

Also noted from a ḥadīth: "Paradise belongs to the muḥakkamūn" — people who, when given the choice between being killed while holding firm to Islam and abandoning it, chose to stand firm and be killed
المُلازَمة — clinging to, keeping close to, adhering.
الحَلِف (verb حَلَفَ / yaḥlifu) — to swear.
a bay mare "not muḥlifa" (not of a doubtful colour, so no one would swear over it)
one root meaning, "opening a thing", and nothing departs from it.
Ḥalāl is the opposite of ḥarām. Ibn Fāris links it to the root as making a thing permissible and leaving it open.
Ḥalla means "he alighted". Ibn Fāris explains that a traveller ties up his baggage and unties it when he halts.
Ḥallaltu al-yamīn means "I released my oath".
Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr: "their striking of the ground is taḥlīl").
highlights.note: Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr, lived into Islam

highlights.text: Imruʾ al-Qays's phrase "wholesome water, not muḥallal" has two explanations.
A ḥadīth says the Prophet married Maymūna "while they were both ḥalāl".
The ḥadīth "No believer loses three children and is then touched by the Fire, except taḥillat al-qasam" is explained through Q 19:71
Al-ḥilm is the opposite of rashness or levity (ṭaysh) — forbearance, self-possession.
ḥalumtu ʿanhu, aḥlumu ("I was forbearing toward him")
Qad ḥalama fī nawmihi ("he dreamed"), verbal noun ḥulm / ḥulum.
Shaving/removing hair from the head, and things derived from that idea.
ḥalaqa (yaḥliqu, ḥalqan) — the ordinary verb "to shave [the head]."

Citation from al-Nābigha: when a commander goes raiding with his army, flocks of carrion-birds (vultures, eagles, crows) are said to circle (ḥallaqa) above it, trailing the army in expectation of the slain who will fall to them
Whatever a person adorns themselves with, made of worked metal or of stones.
On "you eat fresh flesh and extract ornament (ḥilyah) that you wear," Ibn Sīda explains that the statement can be predicated of both bodies of water together because they intermingle
"yuḥallawna fīhā min asāwira min dhahabin wa-luʾluʾan" (they are adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and pearl)
Al-Aghlab al-ʿIjlī's verse describes a girl of Qays b. Thaʿlaba "as though she were the ornament of a gilded sword."
A prophetic report is cited in which the Prophet "used to adorn us with pendant ear-ornaments of gold and pearl."
al-ḥamʾa and al-ḥamaʾ mean black, foul-smelling mud. The Qur'anic phrase min ḥamaʾin masnūn ("from ḥamaʾ masnūn") is cited for the word.
The Qur'an has "he found it setting in a spring that was ḥamiʾa" (Q 18:86).
as in the verse "I said to a doorkeeper beside whom her house stood: 'Give leave, for I am her ḥamʾ and her neighbour'"
the opposite of ذمّ (blame/dispraise), i.e. to praise.
ḥamidtu fulānan / aḥmaduhu — "I praised him / I praise him."
Al-Aʿshā praised al-Nuʿmān b. al-Mundhir with a verse calling him "al-muḥammad" (the much-praised)
one root meaning the lifting or bearing of a thing. Base verb: ḥamala / yaḥmilu / ḥaml ("to carry").
ḥaml — what is borne inside a belly or at the top of a tree: a fetus, or fruit.
ḥiml — a load carried on the back or head.
ḥumūl — camel-litters/howdahs, whether or not women are in them.
cited from Imruʾ al-Qays ("until my tears soaked my sword-strap").
On al-Aʿshā's verse, Ibn al-Sikkīt reports that uḥtumila means "he grew angry."
quoted in a ḥadīth about people leaving the Fire sprouting like seed in a torrent's debris.
he sorts it under five roots: blackening, heat, nearness and presence, a kind of sound, and intent.
Al-ḥamīm is hot water, and al-istiḥmām is washing with it.
From this comes al-yaḥmūm, smoke.
as in Ṭarafa's line about "ashes whose charcoal is effaced".
cited from Abū Dhuʾayb: an angered she-camel withholds her milk "except the sweat, for that oozes".
a single origin — redness (ḥumra) — while allowing that it may be split into two: (1) redness, and (2) a kind of animal (the donkey).
The plain, well-known sense. He cites the Arab saying "beauty is red" (al-ḥusn aḥmar)
Plural forms: ḥamīr, ḥumur, ḥumurāt — patterned, he notes, like ṣaʿīd / ṣuʿud / ṣuʿudāt.
His evidence for the plural al-aḥāmira is al-Aʿshā's line: "the three red things consumed my wealth, and I had long been enamoured of them."
He quotes ʿAlī: "when the fighting turned red [grew fierce] we would shelter behind the Messenger of God, and none of us was closer to the enemy than he."
a core notion of heat, then traces two extensions from it — anger and protection
He cites "a ḥāmiya spring," which he glosses simply as "hot,"
Hence ḥamītu ʿalā fulān, "I burned against him," i.e. I was angry with him. He cites Q 48:26, "the ḥamiyya of the Jāhiliyya."
Q 5:103, "nor a ḥāmī."
he quotes the report "no ḥimā except for God and His Messenger."
